q: Which reagent(s) convert 1-butyne into 2-butanone in one step?
h: Ask which carbon of the triple bond ends up as C=O: the more substituted one (Markovnikov) or the terminal one.
w: Mercury(II)-catalyzed hydration of a terminal alkyne is Markovnikov: OH adds to the internal carbon, and the enol tautomerizes to the methyl ketone. So HgSO4, H2SO4, H2O gives 2-butanone. Hydroboration with a bulky borane is anti-Markovnikov and gives the aldehyde, and ozonolysis cleaves the triple bond.
x: Hydroboration with a bulky dialkylborane puts the oxygen on the terminal carbon; the enol tautomerizes to butanal, an aldehyde, not the ketone.
Lindlar reduction gives 1-butene, and acid-catalyzed hydration of that alkene gives 2-butanol, an alcohol rather than a ketone.
Ozonolysis cleaves the C≡C bond completely, giving propanoic acid and CO<sub>2</sub>, not a four-carbon ketone.

h: The OH must end up on the less substituted alkene carbon. Which addition is anti-Markovnikov and gives an alcohol directly?
w: The target has OH on C2 (the CH end of the alkene), so the addition must be anti-Markovnikov. Boron adds to the less hindered carbon and oxidation replaces B with OH: 1. BH3·THF 2. H2O2, NaOH. Acid hydration is Markovnikov (tertiary alcohol), OsO4 adds two OH groups, and the radical HBr route stops at a secondary bromide that hydroxide mostly eliminates.
x: Acid-catalyzed hydration goes through the tertiary carbocation, giving 2-methyl-2-butanol (Markovnikov), the wrong constitutional isomer.
OsO<sub>4</sub> adds two OH groups (syn dihydroxylation), giving 2-methyl-2,3-butanediol, not a mono-alcohol.
HBr/ROOR does give 2-bromo-3-methylbutane, but this hindered secondary bromide with hydroxide (a strong base) gives mainly E2, back to the alkene, not clean S<sub>N</sub>2.

h: Build the six-carbon skeleton while you still have a terminal alkyne C–H, then choose the reduction that sets the alkene geometry.
w: Deprotonating propyne (pKa ≈ 25) needs a base whose conjugate acid is weaker, such as NaNH2 (NH3, pKa ≈ 38). The acetylide does SN2 on the primary bromide to give 2-hexyne, and Lindlar hydrogenation adds both H atoms to the same face, giving the cis (Z) alkene: 1. NaNH2 2. CH3CH2CH2Br 3. H2, Lindlar.
x: Dissolving-metal reduction (Na, NH<sub>3</sub>) goes through a vinyl radical/anion that adopts the trans geometry, so this gives (E)-2-hexene.
Reducing first gives propene, which has no acidic C–H (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 44), so NaNH<sub>2</sub> cannot form a carbon nucleophile and no C–C bond is made.
Hydroxide (H<sub>2</sub>O pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 15.7) is far too weak to deprotonate a terminal alkyne (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25); the equilibrium lies almost entirely on the alkyne side.

c: 1. H<sub>2</sub>, Lindlar catalyst  2. OsO<sub>4</sub>  3. NaHSO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O
1. H<sub>2</sub>, Lindlar catalyst  2. KMnO<sub>4</sub>, H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat
h: Pair the alkene geometry with the type of dihydroxylation: syn addition to a cis alkene and anti addition to a trans alkene give the same diastereomer.
w: Lindlar reduction gives (Z)-2-butene. OsO4 adds both OH groups to the same face (syn), and syn addition to a cis alkene gives the meso diol, (2R,3S)-2,3-butanediol. So the answer is 1. H2, Lindlar 2. OsO4 3. NaHSO3. Changing either the alkene geometry or the addition mode (syn → anti) switches the product to the racemic (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) pair.
x: Na/NH<sub>3</sub> gives (E)-2-butene; syn dihydroxylation of a trans alkene gives the racemic (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) diol, not meso.
Epoxidation then acid opening is an anti addition; anti addition to the cis alkene gives the racemic diol, not meso.
Hot acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub> cleaves the C=C bond, giving two molecules of acetic acid instead of a diol.

q: The dibromide shown is formed as a racemic mixture (only one enantiomer is drawn). Which sequence from 2-pentyne gives it as the major product?
h: Assign R/S to the drawn dibromide. Then remember Br<sub>2</sub> adds anti, and decide which alkene geometry gives that pair of configurations.
w: The drawn compound is (2R,3R)-2,3-dibromopentane, the threo ("like") diastereomer. Bromination is an anti addition through a bromonium ion. Anti addition to a trans alkene gives the erythro (2R,3S)/(2S,3R) pair (the meso-like pattern seen with 2-butene), while anti addition to a cis alkene gives the threo (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) pair. So the alkyne must first be reduced to the cis alkene: 1. H2, Lindlar 2. Br2, CH2Cl2.
x: Na/NH<sub>3</sub> gives (E)-2-pentene; anti addition of Br<sub>2</sub> to the trans alkene gives the (2R,3S)/(2S,3R) diastereomer, not the one drawn.
HBr with peroxide adds only one Br (radical, anti-Markovnikov), giving a monobromopentane, not a vicinal dibromide.
Two equivalents of HBr add Markovnikov twice to the same carbon, giving geminal dibromides (2,2- and 3,3-dibromopentane), not a 2,3-dibromide.

q: Which sequence moves the double bond of 2-methyl-2-butene to the end of the chain, giving 3-methyl-1-butene as the major product?
h: First put a leaving group on the carbon that must become C2 of the new alkene, then choose a base that removes the less hindered β-H.
w: Radical HBr addition (ROOR) puts Br on the less substituted alkene carbon, giving 2-bromo-3-methylbutane. That bromide has β-H on C1 (CH3) and C3 (one tertiary H). The bulky base t-BuOK removes the more accessible CH3 hydrogen (Hofmann product), giving 3-methyl-1-butene: 1. HBr, ROOR 2. t-BuOK, heat. A small base gives the Zaitsev product, which is just the starting alkene again.
x: Without peroxide HBr adds Markovnikov, giving 2-bromo-2-methylbutane; Hofmann elimination of that gives 2-methyl-1-butene, the wrong skeleton position.
The bromide is correct, but ethoxide is a small base and gives the Zaitsev (more substituted) alkene, which is 2-methyl-2-butene, the starting material.
Hydroboration gives 3-methyl-2-butanol, but E1 dehydration goes through a secondary cation that undergoes a hydride shift to the tertiary cation and gives 2-methyl-2-butene again.

q: Which sequence converts 1-methylcyclohexene into the racemic alcohol shown?
h: Where is the OH relative to the methyl group, and are H and OH added to the same face?
w: The target, trans-2-methylcyclohexanol, has OH on the less substituted alkene carbon (anti-Markovnikov), and the H added to C1 is cis to the OH (syn addition). Hydroboration adds H and B to the same face and oxidation replaces B with OH with retention, so 1. BH3·THF 2. H2O2, NaOH gives the trans alcohol.
x: Oxymercuration–demercuration is Markovnikov: OH goes to the tertiary carbon, giving 1-methylcyclohexanol.
Acid hydration is also Markovnikov through the tertiary cation, giving 1-methylcyclohexanol.
OsO<sub>4</sub> adds two OH groups, giving 1-methyl-cis-1,2-cyclohexanediol, not a mono-alcohol.

q: Which sequence converts acetylene into the racemic diol shown (one enantiomer drawn)?
c: 1. NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br (do this twice)  2. Na, NH<sub>3</sub>(l)  3. OsO<sub>4</sub>, then NaHSO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O
1. NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br (do this twice)  2. H<sub>2</sub>, Lindlar catalyst  3. OsO<sub>4</sub>, then NaHSO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O
1. NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br (do this twice)  2. Na, NH<sub>3</sub>(l)  3. mCPBA, then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
1. NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br (do this twice)  2. H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C  3. OsO<sub>4</sub>, then NaHSO<sub>3</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O
h: The skeleton step is the same in every choice. Assign the drawn diol as meso or chiral, then match alkene geometry with syn or anti dihydroxylation.
w: Two acetylide alkylations with 1-bromopropane give 4-octyne. The drawn diol is (4R,5R)-4,5-octanediol, a chiral (racemic) diastereomer, not the meso form. Racemic comes from syn addition to a trans alkene or anti addition to a cis alkene. Na/NH3 gives (E)-4-octene and OsO4 adds syn, so Na, NH3 then OsO4 gives the (4R,5R)/(4S,5S) pair.
x: Lindlar gives the cis alkene; syn addition to a cis alkene gives meso-4,5-octanediol, not the chiral diol shown.
Na/NH<sub>3</sub> gives the trans alkene, and epoxidation then acid opening is an anti addition; anti addition to a trans alkene gives the meso diol.
H<sub>2</sub> over Pd/C reduces the alkyne all the way to octane, which has no π bond for OsO<sub>4</sub> to attack.

q: Which plan gives 4-methyl-2-pentyne in good yield?
h: An acetylide is a strong base as well as a nucleophile. Which disconnection lets it attack a methyl or primary carbon?
w: Disconnecting the target at either alkyne–carbon bond gives two plans: isopropylacetylide + CH3–X, or propynide + isopropyl–X. Acetylides do clean SN2 only on methyl and primary substrates; with a secondary halide the strong base gives mostly E2. So the good plan is 3-methyl-1-butyne, NaNH2, then CH3I.
x: 2-Bromopropane is secondary; the strongly basic acetylide removes a β-H (E2), giving propene and recovering propyne.
Hydroxide (H<sub>2</sub>O pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 15.7) cannot deprotonate a terminal alkyne (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25), so almost no acetylide forms.
OH<sup>−</sup> is not a leaving group, and the alcohol O–H (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 17) simply protonates the acetylide back to propyne.

q: Which sequence converts methylcyclohexane into racemic trans-2-methylcyclohexanol (shown)?
c: 1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. NaOEt, EtOH, heat  3. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  4. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. t-BuOK, t-BuOH, heat  3. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  4. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
1. Cl<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. NaOEt, EtOH, heat  3. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  4. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. NaOEt, EtOH, heat  3. H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
h: Work backward: which alkene gives this alcohol by hydroboration, which base makes that alkene, and which halogenation puts the leaving group in the right place?
w: Hydroboration–oxidation of 1-methylcyclohexene gives trans-2-methylcyclohexanol (anti-Markovnikov, syn addition of H and OH). 1-Methylcyclohexene is the Zaitsev product of E2 on 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane with a small base, and that tertiary bromide is the highly selective product of radical bromination. So: 1. Br2, hν 2. NaOEt, EtOH, heat 3. BH3·THF 4. H2O2, NaOH.
x: The bulky base gives the Hofmann alkene, methylenecyclohexane, and hydroboration of that gives cyclohexylmethanol instead.
Radical chlorination is not selective; it chlorinates the primary, secondary and tertiary positions, so the later steps start from a mixture of chlorides.
Acid-catalyzed hydration of 1-methylcyclohexene is Markovnikov and gives 1-methylcyclohexanol, the tertiary alcohol.

q: Which C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>12</sub> alkene gives heptane-2,6-dione as the only product of ozonolysis (1. O<sub>3</sub>  2. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>S)?
h: Ozonolysis turns each alkene carbon into a C=O. Reconnect the two carbonyl carbons of the product with a double bond.
w: Heptane-2,6-dione has two ketone carbons (C2 and C6) separated by three CH2 groups, each bearing a CH3. Joining C2 and C6 by a C=C closes a five-membered ring with a methyl on each alkene carbon: 1,2-dimethylcyclopentene. A ring alkene gives one product with two carbonyls; both alkene carbons are fully substituted, so both carbonyls are ketones.
x: 1-Ethylcyclopentene has one alkene C–H, so one end becomes an aldehyde: the product is 5-oxoheptanal.
1,3-Dimethylcyclopentene also has an alkene C–H; it gives 2-methyl-5-oxohexanal, a keto-aldehyde.
1-Methylcyclohexene cleaves to 6-oxoheptanal: the ring is one carbon larger and one end is an aldehyde.

q: Which sequence converts (R)-2-pentanol into the nitrile shown, with the configuration drawn?
c: 1. TsCl, pyridine  2. NaBr, DMSO  3. NaCN, DMSO
h: Assign R/S to the product, then count how many steps break a bond to the stereocenter (each S<sub>N</sub>2 inverts; making a tosylate does not).
w: The product is (S)-2-methylpentanenitrile: the CN has taken the place of the OH with inversion. Tosylation forms the O–S bond and leaves the C–O bond intact (retention), and then cyanide displaces the tosylate by SN2 (one inversion). Net: one inversion, so 1. TsCl, pyridine 2. NaCN, DMSO. Routes with two SN2 steps invert twice and give back the (R) configuration.
x: PBr<sub>3</sub> converts the alcohol to the bromide with inversion, and cyanide inverts again; two inversions give (R)-2-methylpentanenitrile, the enantiomer.
Tosylation retains, bromide displacement inverts and cyanide inverts again: two inversions in total give the (R) nitrile, the enantiomer of the target.
Hydroxide is a very poor leaving group, so cyanide cannot displace OH directly; the alcohol is recovered.

q: Which starting material and reagent give 5-methyl-2-hexanone as essentially the only carbonyl product?
h: Hydration of an alkyne gives a ketone only where the oxygen lands. Which alkyne has only one possible Markovnikov carbon next to the target C=O?
w: Markovnikov hydration of a terminal alkyne puts the oxygen on C2 and gives a methyl ketone: 5-methyl-1-hexyne with HgSO4, H2SO4, H2O gives 5-methyl-2-hexanone. An unsymmetrical internal alkyne has two similar carbons, so its hydration gives a mixture of two ketones.
x: The two alkyne carbons of 5-methyl-2-hexyne are both disubstituted, so oxygen adds to either one: about a 1:1 mixture of 5-methyl-2-hexanone and 5-methyl-3-hexanone.
Hydroboration of a terminal alkyne is anti-Markovnikov and gives the aldehyde, 5-methylhexanal.
Acid hydration of the alkene gives the alcohol 5-methyl-2-hexanol, not a ketone; no oxidation step is present.

c: 1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. t-BuOK, t-BuOH  3. NBS, hν  4. t-BuOK, t-BuOH
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. t-BuOK, t-BuOH  3. NBS, hν  4. H<sub>2</sub>O
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, hν  2. t-BuOK, t-BuOH  3. HBr, ROOR  4. t-BuOK, t-BuOH
h: You need two eliminations, so you need two leaving groups introduced at the right times. Where does NBS put a bromine?
w: Radical bromination and E2 make cyclohexene. NBS then brominates the allylic position (C3) by a radical chain, and a second E2 forms a C=C conjugated with the first: 1. Br2, hν 2. t-BuOK 3. NBS, hν 4. t-BuOK.
x: Water substitutes the allylic bromide (S<sub>N</sub>1 through an allylic cation), giving 2-cyclohexen-1-ol, not the diene.
HBr/ROOR adds across the C=C to give bromocyclohexane again; elimination just returns cyclohexene.
Cyclohexane has no allylic C–H, so NBS is the wrong tool here, and even if one Br were introduced, a single elimination gives only cyclohexene.

q: Using 1-butene and propyne as the only sources of carbon, which plan makes (E)-2-heptene?
c: 1-butene + HBr, ROOR; propyne + NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then add that bromide; then Na, NH<sub>3</sub>(l)
1-butene + HBr; propyne + NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then add that bromide; then Na, NH<sub>3</sub>(l)
1-butene + HBr, ROOR; propyne + NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then add that bromide; then H<sub>2</sub>, Lindlar catalyst
1-butene + HBr, ROOR; propyne + NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then add that bromide; then H<sub>2</sub>, Pd/C
h: Find the C–C bond the acetylide makes, decide which halide the acetylide needs (methyl/primary only), then set the alkene geometry.
w: (E)-2-Heptene is CH3CH=CH(CH2)3CH3. The propynide anion supplies C1–C3 and must attack a primary butyl halide. Radical (peroxide) HBr addition to 1-butene gives 1-bromobutane; SN2 gives 2-heptyne; Na/NH3 reduces it to the trans alkene. So the plan is HBr/ROOR, alkylation of propynide, then Na, NH3(l).
x: Markovnikov HBr gives 2-bromobutane, a secondary halide; the acetylide mostly eliminates (E2), and any substitution would give a branched skeleton.
Lindlar hydrogenation gives the cis alkene, (Z)-2-heptene.
H<sub>2</sub> over Pd/C reduces the alkyne completely to heptane.

q: Three of these routes give cyclohexyl ethyl ether in good yield. Which route gives mostly a different product?
h: In a Williamson-type S<sub>N</sub>2, which carbon should be the electrophile: the primary one or the secondary one?
w: An alkoxide is a strong base. Attacking a primary electrophile (ethyl bromide or ethyl tosylate) it does SN2 cleanly. Attacking a secondary cyclohexyl bromide in hot ethanol it mostly removes a β-H (E2), giving cyclohexene. So bromocyclohexane + NaOEt is the poor route. Alkoxymercuration adds EtOH across the alkene Markovnikov-fashion (both alkene carbons of cyclohexene are equivalent) and also gives the ether.
x: This route works: the cyclohexoxide ion attacks unhindered ethyl bromide by S<sub>N</sub>2.
This route works: alkoxymercuration–demercuration adds H and OCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> across the C=C without rearrangement.
This route works: ethyl tosylate is a primary substrate with an excellent leaving group, ideal for S<sub>N</sub>2 by the alkoxide.

q: Which starting material and reagent give the racemic bromohydrin shown?
h: Halohydrin formation: where does water attack the bromonium ion, and from which face?
w: In Br2/H2O the alkene forms a bromonium ion, and water (the solvent, present in huge excess) opens it at the more substituted carbon, which carries more δ+, from the face opposite the Br. 1-Methylcyclohexene therefore gives 2-bromo-1-methylcyclohexanol with Br and OH trans: 1-methylcyclohexene; Br2, H2O.
x: Methylenecyclohexane gives 1-(bromomethyl)cyclohexanol: Br on the exocyclic CH<sub>2</sub>, not on a ring carbon.
In CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> the only nucleophile is bromide, giving trans-1,2-dibromo-1-methylcyclohexane, not a bromohydrin.
Methanol as solvent opens the bromonium ion, giving the bromo methyl ether (OCH<sub>3</sub> on C1), not the alcohol.

c: 1. Br<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>  2. NaNH<sub>2</sub> (3 equiv), NH<sub>3</sub>  3. H<sub>2</sub>O
1. Br<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O  2. NaNH<sub>2</sub> (3 equiv), NH<sub>3</sub>  3. H<sub>2</sub>O
h: An alkyne needs two eliminations from the same pair of carbons. How many leaving groups must be placed there, and how strong a base does the second elimination need?
w: Br2 gives the vicinal dibromide (1,2-dibromohexane). Two E2 eliminations with NaNH2 give the alkyne; the third equivalent deprotonates the terminal alkyne, and water workup reprotonates it: 1. Br2 2. NaNH2 (3 equiv) 3. H2O. The second elimination (from a vinyl bromide) needs the very strong amide base.
x: HBr installs only one leaving group, so only one elimination is possible, which simply gives back hexene.
Br<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O gives a bromohydrin (only one leaving group); strong base turns it into an epoxide, not an alkyne.
Hydroxide can at most remove one HBr to give a vinyl bromide; it is not strong enough for the second elimination to the alkyne.
